Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Doctor
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event, Authority Presence: Police, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender
  Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

Vignette:
Dr. Linh Tran was fifty-one years old, a married physician who had spent two decades in emergency medicine. She had always believed in the fundamental order of things: that hard work earned safety, that competence protected you, that people were, at their core, predictable. That belief had been destroyed on a Tuesday evening, six months ago, as she walked from the hospital parking garage to her car after a double shift.

The assault had been swift and silent. A man she had never seen before had come up behind her as she unlocked her car door. There had been no shouted threat, no warning—just the sudden pressure of a hand over her mouth, the smell of sweat and something metallic on his skin, and the horrifying intimacy of his body pressed against hers. He had not spoken. That was what she remembered most vividly: the absence of any human sound. The silence itself had become the most terrifying part, because in that silence she had understood that he could do anything, and no one would hear. She had fought, and she had escaped with bruises and a fractured wrist, but something else had been broken that she could not name.

Now, months later, the world had become a place of hidden dangers. Dr. Tran found herself scanning every street corner, every parked car, with a vigilance that exhausted her. The silence that had once been neutral was now a threat. When her husband turned off the television and the house went quiet, her heart would begin to race before she could even identify why. Unexpected sounds—a car backfiring, a dropped tray in the hospital cafeteria—sent a jolt through her chest that left her trembling for minutes afterward. Strangers approaching her in the grocery store aisle made her step backward, her hand instinctively reaching for her keys. She knew this was irrational; she was a doctor, she understood the statistics, she knew the probability of being attacked again was low. But knowing did not stop the terror.

The memory of the event itself had taken on a strange, fragmented quality. When she tried to recall it, she did not see a coherent story but a series of snapshots: the concrete floor of the garage, the fabric of his sleeve, and always, always the smell. The smell would come to her unbidden—in the hospital hallway, in her own kitchen—and suddenly she would be back in that moment, her heart slamming, her throat tight. The terror was as fresh as it had been that evening, and yet the memory felt unreal, as if it had happened to someone else. She would think, *This cannot have happened to me*, even as her body re-lived it.

Dr. Tran had developed a set of strategies to manage the fear, though she would never have called them that. She had stopped wearing the fitted blouses and tailored jackets she had once favored, replacing them with oversized cardigans and loose trousers. She had come to believe that if she made herself smaller, less visible, she would be safer. She had also begun gambling—online poker, late at night, when her husband was asleep. It was not about the money. It was about the focus. When she was in a hand, calculating odds, watching the virtual cards fall, she did not think about the garage. She did not think about the silence. The excitement of a risky bet was the only thing that could drown out the hypervigilance.

Most of all, she avoided any reminder of the man who had harmed her. This was not difficult in the abstract, but it had begun to shape her professional life. She had always worked in the emergency department, but now she found herself avoiding male patients who matched his general build, his approximate age. She would ask a colleague to take over a case, offering a vague excuse about needing a break. She had started requesting shifts in the quieter observation unit, away from the chaos of the ER. Her colleagues had noticed; they had asked if she was alright. She had smiled and said she was fine.

The breaking point had come two weeks ago. Driving home from a late shift, she had passed a police car parked at the side of the road. The officer had been writing a ticket, his body language relaxed, but the sight of the uniform had sent a bolt of pure animal fear through her. She had pulled over, hands shaking, certain that something terrible was about to happen. Nothing happened. The officer did not even look up. But she had sat there for ten minutes, unable to move, her mind flooded with the memory of the garage and the smell and the silence. She had lost faith—in the world, in people, in the God she had never particularly believed in but had always assumed was there. She had lost faith that she could ever feel safe again.

It was her husband who had finally convinced her to call a therapist. She had resisted, because to talk about the event felt like opening a door she had been desperately trying to keep closed. She was certain that if she thought about it directly, she would not be able to hold herself together. But she was not holding herself together anyway. She was a doctor who could no longer work in her own department, a wife who spent her evenings gambling in the dark, a woman who was afraid of silence and strangers and her own memories. She did not know what she hoped for. She only knew that she could not continue as she was.
